headings: What’s the clue; better planning, new technology or just more money? - The area challenge in Norwegian salmon farming
A R T I C L E I N F O

key_figures.quote: In 2019, total production was 1350,000 tons, spread over 966 localities, of which  62 were in active use during the year.
key_figures.statement: The authors report Norwegian salmon production and locality use in 2019: production was 1350,000 tons across 966 localities, with  62 active during the year.

key_figures.quote: This increases the actual area occupation to around 1 4 km2, but still a marginal part of the Norwegian coastal zone.
key_figures.statement: The authors estimate that transport and fishing-distance restrictions increase the occupied area around Norwegian farms to around 1 4 km2.

key_figures.quote: If we use the anchoring area as de facto area occupation, the total equals around 420 km2 or less than 0.5% of the total coastal area available along the coast
key_figures.statement: The authors report an estimate, based on anchoring areas, of Norwegian aquaculture's area occupation as around 420 km2 or less than 0.5% of the available coastal area.

key_figures.quote: A more recent update shows that the area occupation as per 2020 seems to be around 520 km2. (Robertsen pers. comm.), or slightly more than 0.5% of the coastal inshore area.
key_figures.statement: A personal communication cited by the authors estimates aquaculture area occupation in Norway as around 520 km2 in 2020, or slightly more than 0.5% of the coastal inshore area.

key_figures.quote: The Norwegian Food Safety Authority has decided that each farm should have at least 2.5 km to the next farm and minimum 5 km distance to a processing plant.
key_figures.statement: The authors report Norwegian Food Safety Authority distance requirements for farms: at least 2.5 km between farms and minimum 5 km to a processing plant.

key_figures.quote: This implies an area occupation of 20% of the waters in the coastal zone, and this is, in other words, t e most important restriction on furt er growt .
key_figures.statement: The authors report that a cited mapping exercise applying 5 km sanitary zones to localities implies occupation of 20% of coastal-zone waters and identify this as the most important restriction on further growth.

key_figures.quote: Hordaland was top of the list, with 99% of approved localities used over the year, and Finnmark at the bottom, with 73%.
key_figures.statement: The authors report regional differences in the share of approved localities used during the year: Hordaland had 99% and Finnmark 73%.

key_figures.quote: The density of localities in the coastal waters of the counties also spans a large range, from more than four per 100 km2 in Hordaland, to 0.5 per 100 km2 in Finnmark.
key_figures.statement: The authors report county-level locality density ranging from more than four per 100 km2 in Hordaland to 0.5 per 100 km2 in Finnmark.

key_figures.quote: The number of licenses limits growth within this system, and the growth allocated to each of the existing farmers. While licensed capacity is approximately  50,000 tons MAB, the 900 localities are restricted to a total production of ca. 3 million tons MAB.
key_figures.statement: The authors describe Norway's licensed capacity as approximately  50,000 tons MAB and the capacity restriction across 900 localities as ca. 3 million tons MAB.

key_figures.quote: However, around 1 3 of the present localities must lay fallow at any given time, which means that the actual production potential is around 2 million tons MAB
key_figures.statement: The authors estimate that around 1 3 of Norwegian localities must lie fallow at any given time, leaving actual production potential around 2 million tons MAB.

key_figures.quote: So far, 100 standard licenses have been granted to 1  projects, while two projects are still in the pipeline
key_figures.statement: The authors report that Norway's development-license scheme had granted 100 standard licenses to 1  projects, with two projects still in the pipeline.

key_figures.quote: While there were 1 66 localities declared by 1999, the number has been reduced to 966 by 2019.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that declared Norwegian localities declined from 1 66 in 1999 to 966 in 2019.

pq_notes.A0: The authors argue that aquaculture access depends on suitable water conditions, competing coastal uses, municipal plans, sectoral permits and production licences. Although the physical footprint is small relative to the coastal zone, suitable sites are limited and other interests have legal backing or veto powers. Municipalities have a major role under the Planning and Building Act, but multiple sector authorities must also approve localities. The authors identify larger planning areas, auctioned area blocks and marine industrial parks as possible changes that could increase space allocated to aquaculture. They caution that central prioritisation would require major changes to allocation and planning, challenging local democracy. Their assessment is qualitative.
pq_notes.A1: The authors identify site quality, competing uses, planning decisions, production licensing and environmental constraints as interacting influences on development. Companies seek sheltered sites with suitable depth, currents and access to infrastructure; not all coastal waters are therefore interchangeable. Fisheries, transport corridors, tourism, recreation, conservation, energy and military uses also constrain availability. The traffic light system regulates production capacity by production zone according to salmon-lice status, while locality permits require approvals under several sector laws and consistency with municipal plans. The authors find that production-licence capacity, rather than locality capacity, is currently the main national constraint, though availability varies geographically. They also describe alternative production technologies that may reduce demand for coastal sites.
pq_notes.A2: The authors describe a multi-stage locality approval process rather than reporting application-level timings or rejection rates. Operators need a production licence and a locality licence. Counties coordinate and grant the locality permit and full aquaculture licence, but a locality can only be allocated after permissions under relevant sector laws; some sector directorates therefore have de facto veto powers. Sites must also accord with municipal area plans under the Planning and Building Act. Municipalities and authorities may negotiate conflicts, with the Ministry of Local Government and Modernisation deciding if conflicts cannot be resolved. The authors identify complex coordination and limited municipal capacity and competence as planning challenges. They do not provide figures on delays, rejection frequencies or the most common stage of failure.
pq_notes.A3: The authors discuss ecosystem-based management and the need to represent water conditions, ecosystem processes and stakeholder uses in ways that can support decisions. They note that 225 separately planned municipal coastal areas are a poor starting point for ecosystem-based management, and that inter-municipal planning can cover larger areas. Salmon-lice impacts on wild fish became the single indicator used in the traffic light system to determine production growth, stability or reduction across production zones. The authors report a cited mapping exercise in which applying 5 km sanitary zones around localities implied occupation of 20% of coastal waters. This illustrates how farm connectivity and disease precautions can shape area access, but is not presented as a cumulative environmental assessment. They identify limited local knowledge and the need for better understanding of local disease and parasite dispersal conditions.
pq_notes.A4: The authors describe production licences as having been allocated free, later sold at fixed prices and partly allocated by auction; development licences are also granted free if projects meet stated goals. Land-based farming is attractive partly because its licences are in principle free. Municipalities receive little from the earlier property tax on fish pens, while new instruments have been established to distribute more industry wealth to coastal municipalities. The authors assess municipal, county and national costs and benefits, including jobs, value added, environmental impacts and electoral incentives, but this segment does not give a complete numerical distribution. They propose that auctioning area blocks could create an incentive for planning authorities to allocate more areas if auction revenues went to them. Marine industrial parks could use coordination and side payments to internalise effects among commercial activities. These are proposals, not established arrangements.
pq_notes.A5: The authors describe a knowledge base combining social-science research, administrative data, expert judgement and qualitative assessment. Coastal sites must be characterised by temperature, salinity, currents, oxygen supply, depth, exposure and infrastructure, while governance also depends on representing ecosystems and human uses. The authors note that scientific results can be uncertain and that knowledge gaps leave room for negotiation and lobbying. Better local information on currents and the spread of disease and parasites could support more tailored distance rules. Emerging land-based, offshore, closed-pen and large-postsmolt systems may change the need for sea area and the conditions under which salmon are produced. The authors caution that offshore technologies' conclusive results will not be available before 2025-30, and that the technologies may alter Norway's current comparative advantages.
pq_notes.A6: The authors describe conflicts between salmon farming and coastal fisheries, shipping, tourism, recreational and marine tourist fishing, conservation, energy development, military uses, and wild-salmon interests. Some competing uses have strong legal protection, and authorities including the Food Safety Authority, Directorate of Fisheries and Coastal Administration may effectively veto applications. Tourism and fishing users may regard farms as limiting access or spoiling unspoilt landscapes. The authors also report public mistrust of authorities' ability to control environmental impacts, which affects legitimacy and support for growth. They argue that larger planning areas and inter-municipal planning may help accommodate more interests, but note that changing planning units or moving planning upward may be resisted by municipalities. Legitimacy, participation and predictable rules matter, while stronger central prioritisation could challenge local democracy.
pq_notes.A7: The authors identify several industry responses and opportunities to use area more efficiently. Norwegian production increased while the number of localities fell, indicating intensification at existing sites, although this was uneven across the coast. Larger post-smolt produced on land can reduce time spent at sea, salmon-lice exposure and pressure for more marine area, though it requires land and capital investment. Closed sea pens might enable reuse of some abandoned fjord localities if residues such as feed and faeces can be collected and reused; the authors note that current economic analyses do not show that closed pens pay off. Offshore farming may reduce coastal-space pressure if successful. The authors' broader policy argument is that the industry should reduce lice, emissions and escapes and increase legitimacy. These measures are presented as possible routes, not as a single demonstrated solution.
pq_notes.A8: The authors present disease and parasite transmission between farms and impacts on wild fish as important limits on the use of open sea cages. The Norwegian Food Safety Authority's general rules require at least 2.5 km between farms and minimum 5 km to a processing plant. Local currents, land formations, farm size and wild-fish populations vary, and the authors say distance rules might be eased in some places if local conditions and dispersal were better understood. A cited mapping exercise using 5 km sanitary zones around localities implied occupation of 20% of coastal waters. The traffic light system uses salmon-lice frequency as its indicator for production decisions by zone. The authors therefore connect water connectivity and biosecurity both to production limits and to the availability of sites.

headings: A R T I C L E I N F O

key_figures.quote: The paradox raised in the introduction, of having area scarcity when the aquaculture industry is occupying only 0.5% of the coastal areas, can largely be explained by three factors.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that Norwegian aquaculture occupies 0.5% of coastal areas, while noting that perceived scarcity has other causes.

key_figures.quote: A doubling of production by 2030 is theoretically possible within the areas already allocated to aquaculture, while the current growth rate most likely will result in a total production of ca. 2 million tons in 2030.
key_figures.statement: The authors estimate that production could double within already allocated areas by 2030, while the current growth rate would likely yield ca. 2 million tons in 2030.

key_figures.quote: However, after 2030, plans of increasing the present production fivefold towards 2050 will depend on getting access to larger sea areas, gi en t e predominance of t e current production model, based on open net pens.
key_figures.statement: The authors argue that plans to increase Norwegian salmon production fivefold towards 2050 depend on access to larger sea areas under the prevailing open-net-pen model.

key_figures.quote: While economic sustainability for the industry has been extremely successful in this period, generating a resource rent (over and above ordinary profitability) of ca. 20 billion NO  per year over the last few years (NO  2019.1 ), the social sustainability has been more questionable.
key_figures.statement: The authors cite NOU 2019.1 for a resource rent of ca. 20 billion NO per year for the Norwegian aquaculture industry over the last few years.

key_figures.quote: While the report suggested a tax regime similar to that, which had been established in hydroelectric energy production as well as in petroleum, with a 40% tax on profit above the normal, the salmon farmers were against any new tax regime.
key_figures.statement: The authors describe the 40% tax on profits above normal proposed in the 2019 taxation report for the Norwegian aquaculture industry; this is a cited proposal, not an implemented tax.

key_figures.quote: In the end, the government decided to offer the municipalities a production fee of NO  0.40 per kg of salmon.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that the government set a production fee of NO 0.40 per kg of salmon for municipalities.

key_figures.quote: However, the distribution key for the Aquaculture Fund ( a bruksfondet) was changed, to the effect that the municipalities now shall receive only 40% of the income paid for new licenses and new capacity, while the state retain 60%.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that the revised Aquaculture Fund distribution allocates 40% of income from new licenses and capacity to municipalities and 60% to the state.

key_figures.quote: The most ambitious project is being realized in Miami (the  S), where Atlantic Sapphire plans to produce 200,000 tons on land by 2030.
key_figures.statement: The authors cite Atlantic Sapphire’s plan to produce 200,000 tons of salmon on land in Miami by 2030.

pq_notes.A0: The authors argue that where and how much aquaculture can develop depends on sanitary separation between farms, industry preference for “super localities,” competing coastal uses and the perceived legitimacy of the industry. Although farmers report area scarcity, the authors’ analysis suggests considerably more production is possible within the coastal zone, and that some regions are already full. They identify the number of production licenses and the traffic light system, rather than sea space alone, as current constraints. Environmental and social sustainability, and a fairer distribution of costs and benefits, are presented as conditions for legitimate expansion. Planning remains political: zoning and negotiated trade-offs allocate areas among uses, with local politicians assessing risks and benefits.
pq_notes.A1: The authors identify site availability, licensing limits, the traffic light system, sanitary separation and competition with other coastal interests as interacting influences on development opportunities. Farmers claim there is a scarcity of available sea areas, but the authors’ analysis finds room for more production within already allocated areas, while acknowledging that some regions are full. The authors argue that growth is currently constrained primarily by the number of production licenses and strict traffic-light rules, rather than by the total available sea space. Longer-term expansion under the dominant open-net-pen model would require larger areas. Large post-smolt and closed-containment production could reduce the need for new sites, but the economics of closed containment are uncertain.
pq_notes.A3: The authors state that ecosystem-based planning at sea is still in its infancy. They suggest that planning over larger areas could better integrate ecosystem concerns and enable trade-offs, but note that proposals involving counties, production areas or water regions are institutionally weak and lack management measures. The segment does not describe a cumulative-effects assessment method or its formal incorporation into site selection. It does identify uncertainty as a challenge: environmental indicators beyond salmon lice were considered for the traffic light system but dismissed as too uncertain and likely to cause disputes. Digital databases may increase equal treatment and predictability, while ecosystem approaches that include cultural services may produce more variation because local values and preferences differ.
pq_notes.A4: The authors describe the Aquaculture Fund and municipal production fee as economic arrangements intended to compensate municipalities for hosting aquaculture and to improve local incentives. They report that payments cover new licenses and increased capacity, not established farms, and that municipalities consider compensation inadequate. A proposed resource-rent tax of 40% on profits above normal was opposed by salmon farmers and some municipalities and allies, who argued that central collection and existing redistribution schemes would provide little extra locally. The government instead introduced a production fee of NO 0.40 per kg of salmon and changed the Fund allocation so municipalities receive 40% and the state 60% of income from new licenses and capacity. The authors argue that distribution of benefits and costs affects legitimacy and access to space.
pq_notes.A5: The authors say that coastal planning increasingly relies on central digital databases, which they expect to support equal treatment and predictability. They also caution that an ecosystem approach, especially one incorporating cultural ecosystem services, may give greater weight to local values and preferences. A larger factual basis does not remove political judgment: local politicians still assess risks and benefits. The segment discusses technologies that may change spatial needs and environmental impacts. Offshore and land-based farming could reduce demand for inshore areas, but output from these models is expected to remain limited for many years; the authors also note that their wider social and economic effects are not well understood. Large post-smolt may reduce time at sea and salmon-lice problems, while closed containment may reduce environmental problems and permit use of sites abandoned because of local contamination.
pq_notes.A6: The authors identify competing interests including fishers, tourism, recreation and conservation, alongside the political costs municipalities incur in addressing objections. They argue that the coastal zone contains many competing uses, some with exclusive rights, and that the industry’s perceived environmental and social performance shapes its legitimacy. Environmental concerns include fish health, harmful emissions, disease and salmon-lice spread, and escaped farmed salmon; the authors link poor environmental sustainability to limited production growth since 2012. More stakeholder participation is expected, which the authors say will not simplify decisions. They present inter-municipal planning as the most promising planning reform and suggest central guidelines and county support could complement it. Legitimate decisions require negotiated political compromises and a fairer distribution of benefits and costs.
pq_notes.A7: The authors identify operational and technological measures the industry could use to make spatial use more efficient and sustainable. Producing large post-smolt can shorten the period fish spend at sea to market size and may reduce salmon-lice problems. Closed-containment systems may reduce environmental problems and allow the use of sites previously abandoned because of local contamination, although their business economics are uncertain. Offshore or land-based production could reduce demand for coastal inshore areas, but the authors expect their production volume to remain limited for many years. They also argue that industry growth requires improved environmental performance, including better conditions for cleaner fish, and stronger social legitimacy through a better sharing of benefits with municipalities.
pq_notes.A8: The authors identify strict sanitary regulations, including minimum distances between farms, as one of three reasons for apparent area scarcity despite the industry’s small coastal footprint. They also describe disease and salmon-lice spread as environmental concerns affecting the industry’s legitimacy and growth. Salmon lice is the sole indicator used to determine growth in the traffic light system; the authors say adding other environmental indicators was considered but dismissed because of uncertainty and the prospect of disputes. Large post-smolt production is presented as a possible way to reduce time at sea and therefore salmon-lice problems. The segment does not provide details on water connectivity between farms or a method for assessing transmission pathways.
